property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner and any address argument _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) updates C.owner() to equal the provided _owner; the mutant instead sets owner to tx.origin, so for some fuzzed caller/address pairs the final owner differs.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) updates C.owner() to exactly the provided _owner; the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender, breaking this rule when the caller != _owner.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) updates the public owner getter to x; the mutant that omits the assignment breaks this rule because owner remains unchanged for some inputs.
For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) results in C.owner() == x after the call; the mutant breaks this by resetting owner to address(0) regardless of the input.

For any caller address, the original contract only allows the current owner (msg.sender == owner) to successfully call setOwner; the mutant that checks msg.sender == tx.origin can allow non-owner EOAs or disallow legitimate calls when proxied, so there exist inputs where owner after setOwner differs between reference and mutant.

For any caller address A and any newOwner address N, when A directly calls setOwner(N) on the correct contract, the call succeeds iff A == original owner; the mutant that uses tx.origin instead of owner will allow an EOA caller that is not the owner to succeed when proxied through a contract (i.e., a call from a contract with tx.origin == owner but msg.sender == proxy differs), so there exist inputs (a proxy contract caller) where owner after the call differs between reference and mutant.

For any EOA caller directly invoking setOwner(newOwner), only the current owner can change owner (i.e., setOwner succeeds iff msg.sender == owner); the mutant comparing msg.sender==tx.origin can be bypassed by a proxy contract so a non-owner caller through a contract can change owner (violating the rule).

For every caller address that is a contract (i.e., msg.sender is a contract), calling setOwner through that contract must fail to change C.owner unless the contract itself is the current owner (reference enforces msg.sender==owner); the mutant (which compares msg.sender==tx.origin) can be tricked by a proxy contract so a call from a non-owner contract succeeds when tx.origin is the owner, causing owner() to differ.

For any caller address A and target owner address X, if A calls setOwner(X) then after the call the contract's owner equals X (the reference allows the current owner to set owner to any address); the mutant's changed onlyOwner modifier prevents non-zero callers from succeeding, so for some caller A the call will fail to update owner.
